transcript:
This is NPR News Now.
The latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Amy Held.
The FBI has announced North Korea is responsible
for the theft of more than $6 billion in virtual assets
from the cryptocurrency exchange Binance,
the biggest cyber heist in history.
A federal judge has dismissed President Trump's lawsuit
against the Wall Street Journal, as NPR's Stephen Bizaha reports.
It involves a card Trump allegedly sent to the late convicted
sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.
The letter included a drawing of a naked woman
and what appeared to be the president's signature.
The journal reported this in July last year.
Trump denied anything to do with the letter
and called the journal's story fake
and sued for at least $10 billion in damages.
The federal judge dismissed the lawsuit,
declining to rule on whether the actual reporting was false
and saying the president had failed to show
the journal had acted with actual malice.
This is the second time Trump has tried to sue
the Wall Street Journal over this reporting.
The latest case was dismissed with prejudice,
preventing Trump from filing another lawsuit.
Stephen Bizaha, NPR News, Birmingham, Alabama.
Campaigns are making their final push
before Tuesday's midterm elections,
and that means more text messages.
Texas Public Radio's David Martin Davies reports.
Travis Trawick is the founder and CEO of Full Pack,
which specializes in political text messaging.
He says these texts target voters based on their demographics,
political interest, and voting history.
I know precisely who I'm going to engage with.
I can send a message straight to their phone,
directly to their pocket.
Artificial intelligence is also allowing campaigns
to refine their pitches.
You can curate that in so many different ways
and really slice those audiences to be as small as possible.
And as Tuesday approaches,
texting campaigns are becoming more aggressive.
If it becomes too much for you,
voters can reply with the word "stop" to opt out of a list.
For NPR News, I'm David Martin Davies.
Alaska's Republican-led government is urging a federal judge
to dismiss a lawsuit filed at Trump's direction
to stop the certification of a potential Democratic win
in their Senate race.
The Department of Justice wants ballots set aside
to determine whether voters were confused
by two Dan Sullivan's running.
Alaska's Attorney General's office calls that meritless.
An authorized demonstration in Paris has ended for the day.
Hundreds of thousands of people in France
are protesting costs of living and education conditions,
and thousands of police officers are there too,
as unauthorized protesters have in some cases
split off and caused violence.
NPR's Eleanor Beardsley reports from Paris.
It's like a split screen.
If you look at TV right now,
it shows police facing off inside streets
with tear gas against these young people
People wearing hoods and black masks,
and so you feel like it's violent.
Here I am out on a main boulevard
where the march has wrapped up,
and thousands of people are pouring off the boulevard
and they're peaceful.
The rallies have inspired calls for action across Europe.
You're listening to NPR News.
More rain is forecast this weekend in the Southwest,
parts still recovering from severe flooding,
parts of Arizona, Utah, Colorado, and New Mexico
all under flood watches.
Arizona election officials say they're concerned
about the ability of Navajo Nation residents
to reach polling places after floods wiped out roadways.
Ancient Egyptians left clues for how they made mummies,
but they were written in hieroglyphics.
Now archaeologists are helping decipher the code.
NPR's Ping Huang reports.
The ancient Egyptians mummified their dead,
preserving their bodies for thousands of years.
Much of the process remains a mystery,
so researchers at Marburg University in Germany
decided to test samples from mummified heads
and body parts found in museum and historical collections.
Riccardo Guirica, an Egyptologist,
says that chemical analysis turned up substances
new to their understanding of mummification,
like extracts from aloe,
which may shed light on at least one hieroglyphic symbol.
Maybe we can translate anhimi,
which was not very sure beforehand now as aloe.
Aloes surprised them because it wasn't native to ancient Egypt.
It likely came from trade with regions near Ethiopia or Arabia.
The findings are published in the Proceedings
of the National Academy of Sciences.
Ping Huang, NPR News.
The Youth Olympic Games opened in Senegal today,
the first Olympic event in Africa.
About 2,700 athletes aged 14 to 17 compete through November 13.
Russia's delegation is competing under its national flag
for the first time at an Olympic event
since its full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
It's NPR News.

topics.text: FBI attributes $6 billion Binance crypto heist to North Korea, the largest cyber theft ever
Federal judge dismisses Trump's $10 billion lawsuit against the Wall Street Journal over Epstein letter
Campaigns ramp up targeted texting ahead of Tuesday's midterm elections, using AI-refined voter data
Alaska's Republican-led government asks judge to dismiss Trump-directed lawsuit over Senate race certification
Authorized Paris protest over cost of living and education ends; unauthorized splinter groups cause violence
Heavy rain forecast for Southwest flood-damaged areas, with flood watches in Arizona, Utah, Colorado, New Mexico
Arizona officials worry Navajo Nation voters can't reach polls after floods wiped out roads
Researchers find aloe and other new substances in ancient Egyptian mummification, aiding hieroglyph translation
Youth Olympic Games open in Senegal, the first Olympic event held in Africa
Russia's delegation competes under its national flag at an Olympic event for the first time since Ukraine invasion
